title: Solve Factorable Polynomial Inequalities Algebraically
overview: When a polynomial factors, you don't need a graphing calculator to solve its inequality — you can find **exact** answers with algebra. In this section you will review linear inequalities (including the sign flip), then solve polynomial inequalities by considering cases and by using intervals in a sign table, handling negative leading coefficients and squared factors along the way.
objectives: Solve linear inequalities, reversing the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Solve factorable polynomial inequalities by considering all cases.
Solve factorable polynomial inequalities using intervals, test values and sign tables.
Factor polynomials completely before solving inequalities.
Handle negative leading coefficients and repeated (squared) factors.
Represent solutions on number lines and in interval notation, and solve applied problems.

lessons.title: Warm-up: linear inequalities and the sign flip
lessons.body:
Solving a linear inequality is like solving an equation, with **one extra rule**:

> When you **multiply or divide both sides by a negative number**, reverse the inequality sign.

**Why?** Start with a true statement, $2 < 5$. Multiply both sides by $-2$: $-4$ and $-10$. Now $-4 > -10$ — the order has flipped. Multiplying by a negative reflects numbers across $0$ on the number line, so their order reverses.

**Example:** solve $5 - 3x \ge -7$.

$-3x \ge -12$

$x \le 4$ (divided by $-3$, so the sign flipped)

On a number line: a closed dot at $4$ with shading to the left.

Adding or subtracting the same number, or multiplying by a **positive** number, never changes the direction.

lessons.title: Method 1: considering all cases
lessons.body:
A product of **two** factors is

* **positive** when both factors have the **same** sign,
* **negative** when they have **opposite** signs.

**Example:** solve $(x - 2)(x + 4) > 0$.

**Case 1 – both positive:** $x - 2 > 0$ and $x + 4 > 0$ → $x > 2$ and $x > -4$ → $x > 2$.

**Case 2 – both negative:** $x - 2 < 0$ and $x + 4 < 0$ → $x < 2$ and $x < -4$ → $x < -4$.

Solution: $x < -4$ or $x > 2$.

> Within a case, the conditions are joined by **and**, so take the overlap. The cases are joined by **or**, so combine them.

Cases get long quickly: three factors already give four sign combinations to check. That's why the interval method is usually better.

lessons.title: Method 2: intervals and a sign table
lessons.body:
This method works for any number of factors.

1. Factor the polynomial completely and rearrange so one side is $0$.
2. Find the zeros. Mark them on a number line; they split it into intervals.
3. Build a **sign table**: pick a test value in each interval and find the sign of each factor and of the product.
4. Choose the intervals whose sign matches the inequality. Include zeros for $\le$ or $\ge$.

**Example:** solve $(x + 3)(x - 1)(x - 4) \le 0$.

| | $x < -3$ | $-3 < x < 1$ | $1 < x < 4$ | $x > 4$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| test value | $-4$ | $0$ | $2$ | $5$ |
| $x + 3$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x - 1$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x - 4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| product | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Solution ($\le 0$, zeros included): $x \le -3$ or $1 \le x \le 4$.

> You don't always need the full table: one test value per interval in the factored form is enough. The table just keeps your work organised.

lessons.title: Factor first: harder inequalities
lessons.body:
Most inequalities are not given in factored form. Use every factoring tool from Sections 2.2 and 2.3 first.

**Example:** solve $2x^3 + 5x^2 - 18x - 45 \le 0$.

Group: $x^2(2x + 5) - 9(2x + 5) = (2x + 5)(x - 3)(x + 3)$.

Zeros: $-3$, $-\tfrac52$, $3$. Positive leading coefficient, cubic → signs $-, +, -, +$.

Solution: $x \le -3$ or $-\tfrac52 \le x \le 3$.

**Watch out for:**
* **Negative leading coefficients**, e.g. $-x^3 + \dots$ or a factor like $(3 - x)$. Either multiply through by $-1$ (and **flip the sign**!) or track the extra negative in your table.
* **Squared factors**, e.g. $(x + 2)^2$: it is never negative, so it doesn't change the sign — but it is $0$ at $x = -2$, which matters for strict inequalities.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.body:
**Example:** an open-top box is made from a $40$ cm by $32$ cm sheet by cutting squares of side $x$ from each corner. For which $x$ is the volume greater than $2016$ cm³?

* $V(x) = x(40 - 2x)(32 - 2x) = 4x^3 - 144x^2 + 1280x$, with $0 < x < 16$.
* Solve $4x^3 - 144x^2 + 1280x > 2016 \Rightarrow x^3 - 36x^2 + 320x - 504 > 0$.
* $P(2) = 8 - 144 + 640 - 504 = 0$, so $(x - 2)(x^2 - 34x + 252) > 0$.
* Quadratic formula: $x = 17 \pm \sqrt{37} \approx 10.9$ or $23.1$.
* Sign table with zeros $2$, $10.9$, $23.1$: positive on $(2, 10.9)$ and $(23.1, \infty)$.
* Only $0 < x < 16$ makes sense, so $2 < x < 10.9$ cm (approximately $2 < x < 17 - \sqrt{37}$).

keyTerms.definition: A polynomial inequality whose polynomial can be factored, so it can be solved algebraically.
One possible combination of signs of the factors, e.g. both factors positive.
A table showing the sign of each factor and of the product on each interval.
A value chosen inside an interval to find the sign there.

formulas.name: Sign flip

workedExamples.answer: $x > -2$: open dot at $-2$, shading to the right.

workedExamples.title: Using cases
steps: The product is $\le 0$ when the factors have opposite signs (or one is zero).

workedExamples.title: Sign table with a negative leading coefficient
A squared factor
steps: $(x + 2)^2 > 0$ except at $x = -2$ where it is $0$ (and then the product is $0$, not $< 0$).
So we need $(x - 5)(x + 5) < 0$, i.e. $-5 < x < 5$, and $x \neq -2$.

misconceptions.fact: Both factors must have the same sign: both positive **and** together, or both negative together.

misconceptions.myth: Squared factors can be ignored completely.
misconceptions.fact: They don't change the sign, but they make the product $0$ at their zero — exclude that point for $<$ or $>$.
You can't divide by $x$ — you don't know its sign. Use a sign table: $x < 0$ or $x > 3$.

misconceptions.myth: The signs always alternate, starting with $+$ on the left.
misconceptions.fact: The left-most sign depends on the degree and leading coefficient; repeated factors can stop the alternation. Test each interval.

realWorld.title: Manufacturing
realWorld.body: Finding the range of cut sizes that keeps a box's volume above a minimum is a factorable polynomial inequality.

realWorld.title: Safety limits
realWorld.body: Engineers find when a stress or temperature model stays below a safe limit; when the model factors, the exact boundaries come from algebra.

realWorld.title: Profit
realWorld.body: A business is profitable when its profit polynomial is positive; the break-even points (zeros) bound the profitable intervals.

realWorld.title: Exact answers
realWorld.body: Algebraic solutions give exact boundary values (like $17 - \sqrt{37}$), which matter when tolerances are tight.

practice.question: Solve $(x + 2)(x - 4) > 0$ by considering cases.
practice.solution: Both positive: $x > 4$. Both negative: $x < -2$. Solution: $x < -2$ or $x > 4$.

practice.question: Solve $(x - 2)(3 - x)(x - 1) \ge 0$.
practice.solution: Zeros $1, 2, 3$. Leading coefficient $-1$: signs $+, -, +, -$. Solution: $x \le 1$ or $2 \le x \le 3$.

practice.question: Solve $-x^3 + 6x^2 - 9x > 0$.
practice.solution: $-x(x - 3)^2 > 0 \Rightarrow x(x - 3)^2 < 0$. $(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$, so we need $x < 0$ (and $x \neq 3$, automatically true). Solution: $x < 0$.

summary: Reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Factorable inequalities can be solved by **cases** (best for two factors) or by **intervals** with test values (best for three or more).
Always factor completely and get $0$ on one side first.
Include zeros for $\le$ and $\ge$; exclude them for $<$ and $>$.
Squared factors never change the sign but are zero at their root; negative leading coefficients flip the whole sign pattern.

questions.modelAnswer:
A product of two factors is positive when both factors have the same sign.

**Case 1 — both positive:** $x - {{p}} > 0$ and $x + {{q}} > 0$ → $x > {{p}}$ and $x > -{{q}}$ → $x > {{p}}$.

**Case 2 — both negative:** $x - {{p}} < 0$ and $x + {{q}} < 0$ → $x < {{p}}$ and $x < -{{q}}$ → $x < -{{q}}$.

Solution: $x < -{{q}}$ or $x > {{p}}$, i.e. $(-\infty, -{{q}}) \cup ({{p}}, \infty)$.

rubric.point: Correct signs of each factor in the table

questions.text: Solve $(2x - {{a}})(3 - x)(x + {{b}}) \ge 0$. Explain how you handled the factor $(3 - x)$.
questions.modelAnswer:
Zeros: $x = {{a/2}}$, $x = 3$, $x = -{{b}}$.

The factor $3 - x$ has a negative $x$-coefficient, so the leading coefficient of the product is $2 \times (-1) \times 1 = -2 < 0$. (Equivalently, write $3 - x = -(x - 3)$.) The sign pattern of a negative cubic, from the left, is $+, -, +, -$.

| Interval | $x < -{{b}}$ | $-{{b}} < x < {{a/2}}$ | ${{a/2}} < x < 3$ | $x > 3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Check with $x = 0$: $(-{{a}})(3)({{b}}) < 0$ ✓

$$x \le -{{b}} \text{ or } {{a/2}} \le x \le 3$$

rubric.point: Handles $(3 - x)$ correctly (negative leading coefficient or rewriting)
Correct sign pattern with a test value

questions.modelAnswer:
$12x^2 + 25x - 7$: $ac = -84$; $28$ and $-3$ multiply to $-84$ and add to $25$.

$12x^2 + 28x - 3x - 7 = 4x(3x + 7) - 1(3x + 7) = (4x - 1)(3x + 7)$

Zeros $-\tfrac73$ and $\tfrac14$. Parabola opens up → positive outside the zeros.

$$x < -\tfrac73 \text{ or } x > \tfrac14$$

Possible rational zeros: $\pm1, \pm2, \pm3, \pm4, \pm6, \pm12, \pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac13, \dots$

$P(-4) = -384 + 208 + 164 + 12 = 0$, so $x + 4$ is a factor.

Synthetic division with $-4$: $6, 13, -41, 12 \to 6, -11, 3, \mathbf{0}$.

$6x^2 - 11x + 3 = (2x - 3)(3x - 1)$

$(x + 4)(3x - 1)(2x - 3) \le 0$. Zeros $-4, \tfrac13, \tfrac32$; positive cubic → $-, +, -, +$.

$$x \le -4 \text{ or } \tfrac13 \le x \le \tfrac32$$

**Factor.** $P(2) = -48 + 80 + 80 - 80 - 32 = 0$ → $x - 2$ is a factor.
Synthetic division with $2$: $-3, 10, 20, -40, -32 \to -3, 4, 28, 16, \mathbf{0}$.

For $-3x^3 + 4x^2 + 28x + 16$: $Q(-2) = 24 + 16 - 56 + 16 = 0$ → $x + 2$ is a factor.
Synthetic division with $-2$: $-3, 4, 28, 16 \to -3, 10, 8, \mathbf{0}$.

$-3x^2 + 10x + 8 = -(3x^2 - 10x - 8) = -(3x + 2)(x - 4)$

$P(x) = -(x - 2)(x + 2)(3x + 2)(x - 4)$

**Signs.** Zeros $-2, -\tfrac23, 2, 4$. Negative leading coefficient, even degree → down on both ends: $-, +, -, +, -$.

$$-2 \le x \le -\tfrac23 \text{ or } 2 \le x \le 4$$

rubric.point: Finds two zeros using the factor theorem
Factors completely, handling the negative sign

questions.text: Solve $(x^2 + 4x + 4)(x^2 - 25) < 0$. Explain carefully how the squared factor affects your solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
Factor: $(x + 2)^2(x - 5)(x + 5) < 0$.

$(x + 2)^2$ is **never negative**: it is positive for $x \neq -2$ and $0$ at $x = -2$. So it doesn't affect the sign of the product, but at $x = -2$ the product equals $0$, which does **not** satisfy $< 0$.

So we need $(x - 5)(x + 5) < 0$, i.e. $-5 < x < 5$, and also $x \neq -2$.

$$-5 < x < -2 \text{ or } -2 < x < 5$$

rubric.point: Explains that the squared factor is non-negative and doesn't change the sign

questions.text: Solve $9x^2 - {{a^2}} < 0$ and show the solution on a number line.
questions.modelAnswer:
$9x^2 - {{a^2}} = (3x - {{a}})(3x + {{a}})$.

Zeros $\pm\tfrac{ {{a}} }{3}$. The parabola opens upward, so it is negative between the zeros.

$$-\tfrac{ {{a}} }{3} < x < \tfrac{ {{a}} }{3}$$ (about $\pm{{a/3:3}}$)

Number line: open dots at $\pm\tfrac{ {{a}} }{3}$ with shading between them.

Factor: $-x^3 + 6x^2 - 9x = -x(x^2 - 6x + 9) = -x(x - 3)^2$.

$-x(x - 3)^2 > 0$. Multiply by $-1$ and reverse: $x(x - 3)^2 < 0$.

$(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$, and the product is $0$ at $x = 3$. So we need $x < 0$ (where $(x - 3)^2 > 0$ automatically).

$$x < 0$$

rubric.point: Factors completely including the perfect square
Uses the squared factor correctly to reach $x < 0$

questions.modelAnswer:

Zeros $-3$, $-\tfrac52$, $3$. Positive cubic → signs $-, +, -, +$.

$$x \le -3 \text{ or } -\tfrac52 \le x \le 3$$

Number line: closed dot at $-3$ with shading left; closed dots at $-2.5$ and $3$ with shading between.

rubric.point: Finds two zeros and divides correctly

questions.text: Why is it necessary to reverse an inequality sign when each side is multiplied or divided by a negative value? Support your answer with numerical examples and a number-line explanation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Multiplying by a negative number reflects every number across $0$ on the number line, which reverses their order.

* $3 < 7$ is true. Multiply by $-1$: $-3$ and $-7$. Now $-3 > -7$, so the sign must flip.
* $-2 < 4$. Divide by $-2$: $1$ and $-2$; $1 > -2$, flipped again.

On the number line, $3$ is to the left of $7$, but after reflecting across $0$, $-3$ is to the **right** of $-7$. If you kept the original sign you would write a false statement. Multiplying by a positive number only stretches distances, so the order is kept.

rubric.point: At least two correct numerical examples
Contrasts with multiplying by a positive

questions.text: (a) What are the similarities between solving a linear inequality and solving a polynomial inequality? (b) Which is usually more efficient for solving factorable polynomial inequalities algebraically — considering cases or using intervals? Explain with reference to the number of factors.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) **Similarities:** both use the same inequality symbols and notation for solutions (intervals, number lines); both require isolating or rearranging, and reversing the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative; the boundary value(s) come from the related equation. A linear inequality has one boundary point; a polynomial inequality may have several, so its solution can be several intervals.

(b) **Intervals** are usually more efficient. With $n$ factors, considering cases requires checking all sign combinations ($2^n$ in general; already $4$ cases for $3$ factors, $8$ for $4$). The interval method only needs one test value per interval — $n + 1$ intervals for $n$ distinct zeros — and organises naturally in a sign table. Cases are reasonable for two factors.

rubric.point: Chooses intervals with a reason based on the number of factors

questions.text:
A student solved $(x - 2)(x + 4) > 0$ like this:

$x - 2 > 0$ or $x + 4 > 0$, so $x > 2$ or $x > -4$. Answer: $x > -4$.

Find the error, explain why it is wrong (use a test value), and give the correct solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
The student treated the inequality like an equation. For $ab = 0$ we can say $a = 0$ **or** $b = 0$, but for $ab > 0$ both factors must have the **same sign**.

Test value showing the answer is wrong: $x = 0$ is in the student's answer ($0 > -4$), but $(0 - 2)(0 + 4) = -8$, which is **not** $> 0$.

Correct: both positive → $x > 2$; both negative → $x < -4$.

$$x < -4 \text{ or } x > 2$$

rubric.point: Identifies the error (applying the zero product idea to an inequality)
Uses a test value to show the answer fails

questions.text: Write two different quartic inequalities — one using $\ge$ and one using $\le$ — whose solution is $x \le -3$ or $-1 \le x \le 2$ or $x \ge 5$. Show that each one has exactly this solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
The boundary values are $-3, -1, 2, 5$, giving the factors $(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 5)$.

A positive quartic has the sign pattern $+, -, +, -, +$ across $(-\infty, -3)$, $(-3, -1)$, $(-1, 2)$, $(2, 5)$, $(5, \infty)$ — positive exactly on the required intervals.

* **Using $\ge$:** $(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 5) \ge 0$
* **Using $\le$:** multiply by $-1$: $-(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 5) \le 0$ (now the pattern is $-, +, -, +, -$ and we want $\le 0$, the same intervals).

**Check with test values** in the first inequality: $x = 0$ (inside $-1 \le x \le 2$): $(3)(1)(-2)(-5) = 30 \ge 0$ ✓ included. $x = 3$ (outside the solution): $(6)(4)(1)(-2) = -48$, which is not $\ge 0$ ✓ excluded. $x = -2$ (outside): $(1)(-1)(-4)(-7) = -28$ ✓ excluded.
